1.title: Security Concepts and Controls
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Security Concepts and Controls. It covers the exam area General Security Concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The core ideas. Security principles. Control categories. Control types. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: General Security Concepts (sixteen percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: The core ideas
1.text: The core ideas. Confidentiality. Meaning: Only authorized people can read the data. Example: Encrypting a customer file. Integrity. Meaning: Data is accurate and has not been changed without permission. Example: A hash that shows a file was altered. Availability. Meaning: Systems and data are usable when needed. Example: Backups and redundant servers. These three form the C I A triad. Every control protects at least one of them.

1.title: The core ideas, continued
1.text: The core ideas. The figure shows this: The C I A triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability, each with an example control.

1.title: Authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA)
1.text: Authentication, authorization and accounting (A A A). Authentication. Question: Who are you? Example: Password plus an app code. Authorization. Question: What may you do? Example: Read-only access to a share. Accounting. Question: What did you do? Example: Logs of sign-ins and changes. Non-repudiation means a person cannot deny an action. Digital signatures and audit logs give it. Exam tip: Authentication proves identity; authorization grants rights after that; accounting records activity. A digital signature gives integrity and non-repudiation.

1.title: Security principles
1.text: Security principles. Defense in depth: use several layers of controls so one failure does not expose everything. Least privilege: give users and systems only the access needed for the task, and no more. Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. No device or user is trusted because of its network location; every request is authenticated and authorized, and access is continuously evaluated. Separation of duties: no one person controls a whole critical process.

1.title: Control categories
1.text: Control categories. Controls are grouped by how they are implemented. Technical (logical). Meaning: Done by technology. Examples: Firewall, encryption, antivirus, access control lists. Managerial (administrative). Meaning: Policies and oversight. Examples: Risk assessments, security policies, awareness programs. Operational. Meaning: Done by people in daily work. Examples: Guards, security awareness procedures, backup routines. Physical (environmental). Meaning: Protect buildings and equipment. Examples: Locks, fences, badges, cameras, fire suppression.

1.title: Control types
1.text: Control types. Controls are also grouped by what they do. Preventive. Purpose: Stops an incident. Examples: Firewall rule, door lock, patching. Deterring. Purpose: Discourages an attacker. Examples: Warning signs, visible cameras, banners. Detective. Purpose: Finds an incident that happened. Examples: I D S alerts, log review, motion sensors. Corrective. Purpose: Fixes the damage or restores. Examples: Restoring from backup, patching after an attack.

1.title: Control types, continued
1.text: Control types. Compensating. Purpose: Substitutes when the main control cannot be used. Examples: Extra monitoring on a legacy system that cannot be patched. Directive. Purpose: Instructs what must be done. Examples: Policies, procedures, standards. Exam tip: A compensating control is a substitute for a control that cannot be used. A corrective control happens after the event. Do not confuse them.

1.title: Control types, continued
1.text: Control types. The figure shows this: A matrix of control categories and control types with one example for each. Exam tip: Ask two questions: how is it implemented (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and what does it do (preventive, deterring, detective, corrective, compensating, directive). A camera is physical and detective (and also deterring). A policy is managerial and directive.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors adds a banner that warns that all activity on its network is monitored. Which control type is mainly shown? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Deterring. A warning banner discourages misuse, which is a deterring control. It does not stop or fix anything.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A legacy server cannot be patched, so the team places it on an isolated segment with extra logging. Which control type is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Compensating. The isolation and logging substitute for patching that cannot be done, so they are compensating controls.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company writes an acceptable use policy that tells staff what they must and must not do. Which category and type fit best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Managerial and directive. A policy is a managerial control that directs behavior, so it is a directive control.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which concept is provided by a digital signature on a signed contract? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Integrity and non-repudiation. A signature shows the content was not changed (integrity) and the signer cannot deny signing it (non-repudiation).

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An administrator gives a help desk analyst only the rights needed to reset passwords. Which principle is applied? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Least privilege. Granting only the access needed for the task is least privilege.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A user signs in and the system then checks which files the user may open. Which step of A A A is the file check? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Authorization. Deciding what the authenticated user may access is authorization.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What are the three parts of the C I A triad? Answer: Confidentiality, integrity and availability. Question two. What does A A A stand for? Answer: Authentication, authorization and accounting. Question three. Name the four control categories. Answer: Technical, managerial, operational and physical.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name the six control types. Answer: Preventive, deterring, detective, corrective, compensating and directive. Question five. What is the slogan of Zero Trust? Answer: Never trust, always verify. Question six. What does non-repudiation prevent? Answer: A person denying an action they performed.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. C I A: confidentiality (secret), integrity (unchanged), availability (usable). A A A: who you are, what you may do, what you did. Principles: defense in depth, least privilege, Zero Trust (verify every request). Categories: technical, managerial, operational, physical. Types: preventive stops, deterring discourages, detective finds, corrective fixes, compensating substitutes, directive instructs. In the next module, we continue the course.
